lines.text: Circuit symbols let any reader identify components without seeing the apparatus.

Recall and use the standard circuit symbols in section six of the syllabus. A cell has a long and short parallel line, several pairs form a battery. A fixed resistor is a rectangle, a variable resistor has a diagonal arrow. A lamp has a cross in a circle, an ammeter ay in a circle, and a voltmeter V in a circle. Recognise the standard forms for an open or closed switch, diode, light dependent resistor, thermistor and oscilloscope. Preserve polarity where the symbol gives it.
Once each symbol is recognisable, follow the wires and junctions to interpret the circuit.
Use the section six symbols consistently. A cell is one long and one short line. ay and V inside circles denote meters.
How would you distinguish a cell from a battery and a fixed from a variable resistor?
A circuit picture tells you which parts share a current or a potential difference.

Draw and interpret circuit diagrams using the section six symbols. Trace continuous conducting paths and mark junctions clearly. A crossing without a junction is not an electrical connection. Series components lie on one path and share current, parallel components connect between the same two junctions and share potential difference Put an ammeter in series with the component whose current is needed. Put a voltmeter across the two points whose potential difference is needed. An open switch breaks its path.
Correctly locating a voltmeter across the source lets you identify terminal potential difference.
Trace wires through marked junctions. Ammeter, series. Voltmeter, across two points. Open switch, broken path.

A voltage rating tells how much energy a source supplies to each coulomb.

Define the electromotive force, E M F, of a source as energy transferred per unit charge in driving charge around a complete circuit. In symbols, E equals W over Q, where W is energy supplied to charge Q. Thus W equals E Q. The volt is one joule per coulomb. The energy supplied by the source includes energy subsequently dissipated inside the source as well as in the external circuit.
Compare that total supply per charge with the energy transferred per charge across one component.
E equals W over Q, energy per unit charge. The charge goes around a complete circuit. Unit, joules per coulomb or V.
What does a nine point zero volts label tell you about energy supplied to each coulomb?
Equal numbers in volts can describe different stages of the energy journey.

Distinguish E M F from potential difference by energy transfer. E. m. f. is energy supplied by the source per unit charge around the complete circuit, often from chemical to electrical energy. P. d. across a component is energy transferred from electrical energy to other forms per unit charge in that component. A resistor transfers it mainly to thermal energy, a lamp transfers it to light and thermal energy. Both are measured in volts, or joules per coulomb. Terminal potential difference measures the energy per charge available to the external circuit.
Internal resistance explains why terminal potential difference can be below source E M F.
E. m. f. supplied energy per charge. P. d. transferred energy per charge. Both use volts.
Why can E M F and resistor potential difference have the same value yet describe different transfers?
A source can read less across its terminals while delivering current.

A real source has internal resistance r. Current I produces an internal potential difference I r called lost volts. For a discharging source, E equals V plus I r, so terminal potential difference V equals E minus I r. Increasing current at fixed E M F and internal resistance raises the internal energy dissipated per unit charge and lowers terminal potential difference At zero current, the lost volts are zero and V equals E. Raising external resistance usually lowers current, so terminal potential difference rises towards E M F A voltmeter across the source terminals reads V.
This relationship prepares you to apply circuit laws to complete loops and networks.
Lost volts across internal resistance, I r. Terminal potential difference, V equals E minus I r. At I equals zero, V equals E.
Why does adding a parallel load often lower the voltmeter reading across a real cell?

ten point one Practical circuits.
In one breath.

A source gives energy to each coulomb of charge as it drives it around a complete circuit. Some of that energy can be transferred inside the source, leaving less per coulomb available at its terminals.
Key ideas.

Learn the standard symbols in section six of the syllabus and use them consistently. A cell has one long and one short parallel line, a battery has multiple such pairs. A fixed resistor is a rectangle, and a variable resistor adds a diagonal arrow. An ammeter is a circle with ay, a voltmeter is a circle with V. Recognise the prescribed symbols for switches, lamps, diodes, light dependent resistors, thermistors and the oscilloscope as well. Draw straight wires and clear junctions. A crossing with no junction dot does not connect branches.

A circuit diagram records electrical connections, not the physical position of equipment on a bench. Trace a continuous loop from one source terminal to the other to decide whether current can flow. Components in series share a path and the same current. Components in parallel connect to the same two junctions and have the same potential difference. An ammeter must be in series with the component whose current it measures, a voltmeter connects across the two points whose potential difference it measures.

The electromotive force, or E M F, of a source is energy transferred per unit charge in driving charge around a complete circuit, E equals W over Q. The unit is the volt, equivalent to a joule per coulomb. A battery marked nine point zero volts supplies nine point zero joules per coulomb to the whole circuit. That label does not promise nine point zero joules per coulomb to the external components alone.

Potential difference across a component is energy transferred from electrical energy per unit charge in that component. For a resistor, this energy usually becomes thermal energy, for a lamp it can become light and thermal energy. E. m. f. describes energy supplied per charge by the source, whereas potential difference describes energy transferred per charge across a component. Both have the same unit even though they describe different energy transfers.

A real source has internal resistance r. When it supplies current I, energy per charge I r is dissipated internally. Its terminal potential difference is therefore. V equals E minus I r. The term I r is called the lost volts. At zero current, I r equals zero and terminal potential difference equals E M F At greater current, lost volts rise and terminal potential difference falls if E and r stay fixed. If the external resistance rises, current often falls and terminal potential difference rises towards E.
Method.
Read the circuit topology, find the source, its internal resistance, junctions, and the path of current. Place an ammeter in series and a voltmeter across the relevant two points.
For an energy question, use E equals W over Q or W equals E Q and include the complete circuit in your interpretation.

For terminal potential difference, write E equals V plus I r first. Substitute with volts, amperes and ohms, then state the answer in volts. Check that a discharging cell with nonzero current has V is less than E.
Worked example.

A cell has E M F twelve point zero volts and internal resistance zero point five zero omega. It supplies two point zero amperes. Calculate its terminal potential difference Write V equals E minus I r because the internal potential difference uses some of the supplied energy per charge. V equals twelve point zero minus two point zero times zero point five zero equals eleven point zero volts. The result is below the E M F, as expected for a source supplying current.
Traps.
Trap, Put the voltmeter in series. Why it's wrong, It must compare two points. Instead, Connect it across the component or source terminals.
Trap, Treat a battery's E M F as the external potential difference under load. Why it's wrong, Charge transfers energy inside the source. Instead, Subtract I r.
Trap, Say E M F or potential difference is an amount of energy. Why it's wrong, Both are energy per unit charge. Instead, State the ratio and the energy transfer involved.
Exam technique.

For Define, include energy transferred per unit charge and the complete circuit. For Explain questions about changing terminal potential difference, say how current changes, then how I r changes, then use V equals E minus I r. In diagram questions, trace actual joined wires, nearby symbols or crossed wires do not automatically form a conducting path.
